name: Anti-estrogen diet (cruciferous / DIM)

lead: The anti-estrogen diet means eating more cruciferous vegetables or taking DIM, a compound derived from them, in the belief that it lowers estrogen and favours testosterone.
Cruciferous vegetables are studied for cancer and detoxification enzymes. The sources reviewed describe no clinical trial testing the hormone claim.

paras: DIM forms when indole-3-carbinol from these vegetables is digested. Lab studies show it acts on several cell pathways, but how this translates to estrogen levels in men has not been shown in published trials found here.
Pure DIM carries irritation hazard labels; supplement safety trials are not described in the sources. It is sold as a dietary supplement.

lead: The anti-estrogen diet is a lifestyle practice in which people eat cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage, kale and Brussels sprouts, or take supplements of diindolylmethane (DIM), with the stated aim of lowering estrogen activity or shifting estrogen metabolism, usually in order to raise the ratio of testosterone to estrogen. DIM is a compound formed in the body from indole-3-carbinol, which comes from these vegetables, and it is sold as a dietary supplement.[1]

Research on cruciferous vegetables has centred on glucosinolates and their breakdown products, studied mainly for cancer prevention. An umbrella review reported suggestive evidence of benefit for some cancers and all-cause mortality, and the vegetables are known to induce the liver enzyme CYP1A2.[2] The Wikipedia articles on DIM and cruciferous vegetables do not describe any trial showing that these foods or DIM change estrogen levels or appearance in men.

paras: Practitioners add cruciferous vegetables to meals or take DIM capsules. DIM arises when indole-3-carbinol from the vegetables is digested, and the compound is marketed as a supplement.[1]

Laboratory work cited on Wikipedia reports that DIM inhibits certain histone deacetylases in vitro and acts as a weak cannabinoid receptor agonist, and a 2003 study examined DIM as an androgen antagonist in human prostate cancer cells.[1][2] These are cell-based findings and do not establish effects on estrogen in healthy men.
Cruciferous vegetable research is mostly about cancer and enzyme induction rather than sex hormones; the cruciferous vegetables article does not mention estrogen.[2]

No studies found. Wikipedia notes that, as of 2025, no clinical trials had confirmed DIM's effectiveness for its one tested human-use claim (reducing dental plaque), and the articles describe only laboratory and observational research on the compound and the vegetables.[1][2]
The chemical hazard classification for DIM lists skin, eye and respiratory irritation warnings for the pure substance.[1] Wikipedia's articles do not describe human safety trials of DIM supplements.
